title: Madeira Cake
subtitle: a dense, close-crumbed lemon loaf with a crisp top
excerpt: Madeira cake is a firm, buttery loaf with a tight crumb and a clean lemon flavour. It is less sweet than most cakes and holds its shape when sliced. Traditionally served with a glass of Madeira wine, it is now simply a classic British loaf cake.
sourceNotes: A British Victorian cake, named not because it contains Madeira wine but because it was traditionally served alongside it.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freezes well. Wrap tightly and defrost at room temperature.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps for 4 to 5 days in an airtight tin. It improves on the second day.
recipe.temperatureNote: Conventional oven -- low and slow for a close crumb

content.text: Cream the butter and sugar for longer than you think necessary -- 5 full minutes until very pale and doubled in volume. This air is what makes the tight crumb of a Madeira cake. Add the eggs slowly to avoid curdling.
Heat the oven to 160C. Grease and line a 900g loaf tin.
Beat the softened butter, caster sugar, and lemon zest together for 5 minutes with an electric whisk until very pale and fluffy.
Beat in the eggs one at a time, adding a tablespoon of flour with each one to prevent curdling.
Fold in the remaining flour and baking powder. Add the milk and fold until just combined.
Pour into the tin. Bake for 55 to 65 minutes until a skewer comes out clean and the top is golden with a crack along the length. Cool in the tin for 10 minutes, then turn out.

items.cause: Not enough air beaten into the butter and sugar, or the eggs were added too quickly and the batter curdled.
items.fix: Beat the butter and sugar for the full 5 minutes. Add eggs slowly and add a spoonful of flour if the mixture looks greasy.
A Madeira cake should have a close, firm crumb but not dry out. Check with a skewer at 55 minutes and remove as soon as it comes out clean.

content.text: Madeira cake is a Victorian British classic. Its firm texture made it practical -- it sliced neatly, kept well, and sat politely alongside a fortified wine. Today it is simply a reliable, unshowy loaf cake. It is the kind of cake that sits on the counter all week and improves slightly with each passing day.
